newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia crude oil prices bounce lightly, seen bearish.
newsitem.headline: Asia crude oil prices bounce lightly, seen bearish.

text.p: Crude oil prices in Asia inched up on Thursday after plunging overnight, but prices were likely to remain under pressure from a combination of bearish factors, including resumed Iraqi crude oil exports.

Traders said the Iraqi deal, weak oil product futures, forecasts for mild weather in the United States and an unexpected build-up in U.S. gasoline and distillate stocks were likely to weigh on the market.
"I can't be sure, but my gut feeling is that perhaps we've reached the end of the bull run that's been driving the crude market," one trader with a leading Japanese oil company said.
He said Thursday's bounce in crude oil prices, after the previous day's tumble of more than $1.00 a barrel, was anemic compared with the rebounds that followed sell-offs earlier in the year.
"We've had oil prices falling before this year...but the market's recovery has usually been very steady. It's usually bounced back," he said.
Crude oil prices on average this year have remained about $3.00 a barrel above comparable periods last year, due in part to the absence of Iraqi crude oil from global markets.

But under a recently approved U.N. oil-for-food scheme, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months in order to buy food and medicine for civilians suffering under sanctions imposed by the U.N. after Baghdad invaded Kuwait in 1990. At current prices exports are expected to be about 550,000 barrels per day (bpd).
Since the deal's start on Tuesday, a total of five crude oil contracts have been posted to U.N. overseers. One has been approved and four turned back.
The return of Iraqi crude oil had long been anticipated and many traders held the view that the eventual flow of Iraqi crude was already factored into the market.
Wednesday's rout in the markets, however, suggested that market sentiment on Iraq may be changing.
January cash Brent was notionally assessed in Tokyo at $22.15/22.25. while on SIMEX January Brent crude futures were untraded but quoted at $22.17/22.35 per barrel during late Asian business hours.

On London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) on Wednesday, benchmark January Brent Blend crude from the North Sea tumbled $1.13 to close at $22.16 a barrel, after hitting an intraday low of $22.00.

The New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) January crude oil futures, another global benchmark, were traded in late Asian hours on the after-hours ACCESS screen-based system at $23.38, unchanged from New York's Wednesday close, which was off $1.04 from the prior session.
Some brokers also said the decline in oil product futures was dampening crude oil trading.
Singapore gas oil prices fell sharply on Thursday along with the big losses on crude and gas oil values on the IPE, despite unchanged Asian fundamentals.
